title: AutoScientist-Quant: Self-Evolving Coding Agents for Automatic Research in Quantitative Investment
content:
Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence
  [Submitted on 5 Aug 2026]
    Title:AutoScientist-Quant: Self-Evolving Coding Agents for Automatic Research in Quantitative Investment
View PDF HTML (experimental)
            Abstract:Large language model agents can discover alphas, yet current methods have three weaknesses. The search cannot adapt during the run, automation usually ends at alpha generation while library selection and model choice stay manual, and alpha discovery can read the test window through loop feedback or code problems. We present AutoScientist-Quant, a self evolving search process that regards quantitative research as one budgeted search problem. A single controller conditions every decision on the remaining budget, choosing at each round whether to improve, combine, pivot, or stop, which node to expand, how many alphas to generate, and how to retrieve past trajectories from the shared memory. The same core then selects from the library and tunes the model, closing the loop from hypothesis to deployable strategy. We also review the evaluation pipeline reused from prior work, fix two lookahead problems, and keep the feedback window disjoint from the held out test window, so every comparison tests true generalization. On CSI universes, the framework attains the best value of nearly every metric in every setting, and these conclusions hold across several backbones and markets.

report.summary: A new framework uses self-evolving coding agents to automate quantitative investment research, improving alpha discovery and preventing data leakage.
report.background: Quantitative investment relies on discovering alpha factors that predict market movements. While large language model agents can generate alpha candidates, existing approaches have three critical weaknesses: they cannot adapt their search strategy mid-run, they stop after alpha generation without automating library selection and model tuning, and they risk leaking test-window information through loop feedback or coding errors. AutoScientist-Quant reframes the entire quantitative research workflow as a single budgeted search problem. A central controller decides at each step whether to improve, combine, pivot, or stop, based on the remaining compute budget. It also selects which nodes to expand, how many alphas to generate, and how to reuse past trajectories from shared memory. By extending the same core to choose libraries and tune models, the system closes the loop from hypothesis to deployable strategy. The authors also fix two lookahead problems and keep feedback and test windows disjoint, ensuring true generalization.
key_points: AutoScientist-Quant treats quantitative research as one budgeted search problem. A single controller conditions every decision on the remaining budget, choosing whether to improve, combine, pivot, or stop. This adaptive approach contrasts with earlier methods that use fixed search policies and cannot adjust during a run, making it more efficient and flexible.

The framework automates the full pipeline, not just alpha generation. The same core selects factor libraries and tunes models, producing deployable strategies. This eliminates the manual handoff that normally follows alpha discovery, reducing human effort and enabling end-to-end autonomous research in quantitative investment.

It fixes two lookahead problems and enforces strict data separation. The feedback window is kept disjoint from the held-out test window, preventing contamination and loop leakage. As a result, performance metrics reflect genuine out-of-sample generalization rather than accidental overfitting or data snooping.

On CSI universes, AutoScientist-Quant achieves the best value of nearly every metric in every setting, and the results hold across multiple backbones and markets. This demonstrates that the framework is robust and not tied to a specific model, suggesting broad applicability in quantitative finance and beyond.

By framing research as a budgeted search problem with memory retrieval, the paper offers a blueprint for self-evolving agents that can manage long-horizon tasks. This design could inspire similar systems in other scientific fields where automated hypothesis generation, experimentation, and model tuning need to coexist under resource constraints.
report.impact: For the AI industry, AutoScientist-Quant demonstrates that LLM agents can manage complex, multi-stage research workflows with adaptive budget allocation and memory reuse. This could push agentic AI beyond simple tool calling into autonomous scientific discovery. Developers can learn from the controller design and the strict evaluation discipline to build more reliable research automation systems. For quantitative finance, it promises more robust alpha generation and reduced overfitting, potentially improving fund performance and risk management. Regular users may see this as a step toward AI-managed portfolios that are less reliant on manual quant researcher oversight. However, because the paper relies on simulated or historical market data, real-world deployment still requires careful validation and regulatory compliance.
report.tools: As of this writing, no official code repository is linked in the abstract. Readers interested in implementation details should monitor the arXiv page and search GitHub, Hugging Face, and DagsHub for open-source releases. For tracking related literature, Connected Papers and Litmaps can help map citation networks around LLM agents and quantitative finance. alphaXiv provides a useful platform for discussing and annotating the paper with other researchers.
